text.p: ABB Asea Brown Boveri AG's better-than-expected first quarter results surprised and comforted analysts and its shares are likely to rebound in the short term after a recent slump.
Analysts' positive view of ABB contrasts with the sombre mood that prevailed only two months ago when disappointing 1996 results triggered downgradings and earnings reductions.
While many analysts are taking a second look at their ABB forecasts, most caution that markets should not get carried away by the the first quarter results.
"It's good news and a pleasant surprise after the negative surprise after the 1996 numbers," said Glen Liddy of Kleinwort Benson Securities.
"But it's only one quarter and you can't extrapolate for the entire year. We'll see if this is sustainable," Liddy added.
Many analysts will decide whether to change or stick with forecasts after a Thursday telephone conference with ABB.
ABB disappointed analysts and markets in February when it announced a 16 percent increase in comparable 1996 net profit to $1.233 billion.
The shares of its Swiss-quoted parent ABB AG fell from 1,810 Swiss francs before the result to a low of 1,667 francs in the following days and has only gradually clawed back some ground.
But after Tuesday's result the share gained two percent and some analysts expect it to rebound to recent year-highs.

Francine Lenoir of Societe General Bank & Trust sees a potential upside of 10 percent in the shares of Swiss ABB AG and Sweden's ABB AB based on expected good earnings news in the second half and speculative appeal linked to possible spin-offs and share buy-backs.
ABB's results mainly surprised on two counts: Strong orders and higher operating margins.

In addition, analysts took heart from ABB's confirmation of its profit forecast for 1997 and comments by Goran Lindahl, ABB chief executive and president, about the forecast effectively setting a floor for his profit expectations.
"The forecast is conservative, it merely sets a floor. Lindahl will not want to start his job as new chief executive by disappointing markets," said one Swedish analyst.
Lindahl told Reuters the 1997 forecast for profits to at least reach the 1996 level was "definitely a floor and no ceiling whatsoever" and "I have some confidence in that floor."

ABB's first quarter net profit rose eight percent to $236 million and 14 percent in local currencies. Operating profit rose 11 percent in dollar terms to $472 million and 17 percent in local currency terms.
On average analysts had forecast net profit of $223 million with a range from $213 to $240 million.
ABB's results surprised on two counts: Orders and margins.
First quarter orders rose 16 percent in dollar terms and 22 percent in local currency terms to $10.08 billion.
"There was a much better contribution from emerging markets than expected," said Andrew Griffin of UBS, referring to orders.
Even Lindahl was satisfied with the results, adding the order intake was "promising for the future."
However, other analysts noted that orders were inflated by large projects and the important orders for standard products were slightly down.
"Obviously it's good orders are up significantly, but it is not a great indicator of what can be expected for the rest of the year," one London analyst said.
First quarter operating margin rose to 6.7 percent from 5.8 percent and 1996's restated 6.6 percent.
While the improvement is minor, it is significant because represents a turnaround from last year when the margin declined.
Lenoir said the improvement in operating margin was partly driven by better margins at power generation.
"However, the best is yet to come for this business which was completely restructured and is likely to benefit from a more favourable price environment," Lenoir said.
Peter Naeslund of Handelsbanken in Sweden added that ABB's first quarter profits were a positive surprise.
"It shows that costs are coming down and signals to everyone that has been scared about power generation that it now has stabilised," Naeslund said.
